title: No Ternary Operator
summary: Go has no ?: operator, so learn the idiomatic if/else assignment, default-then-override, and switch patterns instead.
intro: Many languages let you write `cond ? a : b` to pick a value. Go leaves it out on purpose. Nested ternaries get hard to read, and Go prefers one clear way to write things. This lesson shows the three patterns Go programmers use instead.

steps.title: Assign in if/else

example.title: Parity and plurals
example.prompt: Pick a word for a number's parity and a singular or plural word for a count, then print both.
example.explanation: `var parity string` starts as `""`. Since `14%2 == 0` is true, the first branch assigns `"even"`. The same pattern picks `"item"` because `count` is exactly 1. `fmt.Println` joins its arguments with spaces.

practice.title: Pass or fail
practice.prompt:
Pick a result for a score and a singular or plural word for a point difference.

1. Declare `var result string` and set it to `PASS` when `score` is 60 or more, otherwise `FAIL`. Print it.
2. Declare `var word string` and set it to `point` when `diff` is 1, otherwise `points`.
3. Print `diff` and the word on one line, separated by a space.

Expected output:

```text
FAIL
2 points
```
hints: Declare the variable before the if, then use `=` (not `:=`) in both branches.

steps.title: Default, then override
steps.body:
When one outcome is the usual case, start the variable at that default and override it with a single `if`. There is no `else` to write:

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	total := 60
	{{code}}
	fmt.Println("fee:", fee)
}
```

```go
fee := 5
if total >= 50 {
	fee = 0
}
```

The same trick finds the larger or smaller of two values. Assume the first one wins, then switch when the second beats it:

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a, b := 7, 12
	{{code}}
	fmt.Println(bigger)
}
```

```go
bigger := a
if b > a {
	bigger = b
}
```

Go 1.16 has no built-in `max` or `min` (they arrived in Go 1.21), so this is the pattern you will write. Later, the functions lessons wrap it in helpers like `maxInt`.

With three or more outcomes, a chain of overrides gets confusing. Use a `switch` with no value: the first true case wins, so with `<` and `<=` checks order the ranges from low to high, as in the if-else lesson, and let `default` catch the rest.

```go harness
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	t := 18
	var label string
	{{code}}
	fmt.Println(label)
}
```

```go
switch {
case t < 10:
	label = "cold"
case t <= 25:
	label = "mild"
default:
	label = "hot"
}
```

example.title: Status, larger value, and level
example.prompt: Pick an open or closed status, the larger of two numbers, and a low, ok, or high label, then print all three.
example.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	hour := 10
	status := "closed"
	if hour >= 9 && hour < 17 {
		status = "open"
	}
	fmt.Println(status)

	a, b := 7, 12
	bigger := a
	if b > a {
		bigger = b
	}
	fmt.Println(bigger)

	reading := 72
	var level string
	switch {
	case reading < 60:
		level = "low"
	case reading <= 80:
		level = "ok"
	default:
		level = "high"
	}
	fmt.Println(level)
}
example.explanation: `status` starts as `"closed"` and the one `if` overrides it because 10 is between 9 and 17. `bigger` starts at 7 and becomes 12 because `b > a`. In the switch, `72 < 60` is false and `72 <= 80` is true, so `level` is `"ok"` and the remaining cases are skipped.

practice.title: Fee, smaller, speed
practice.prompt:
Pick a shipping fee, the smaller of two numbers, and a speed label, then print all three.

1. Start `fee` at 5 and override it with 0 when `total` is 50 or more. Print `fee`.
2. Start `smaller` at `x` and override it with `y` when `y` is less than `x`. Print `smaller`.
3. Use a switch with no value to label `speed` as `slow` (under 40), `normal` (40 to 90), or `fast` (over 90). Print the label.

Expected output:

```text
0
4
fast
```
practice.solution:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	total := 64
	fee := 5
	if total >= 50 {
		fee = 0
	}
	fmt.Println(fee)

	x, y := 9, 4
	smaller := x
	if y < x {
		smaller = y
	}
	fmt.Println(smaller)

	speed := 95
	var label string
	switch {
	case speed < 40:
		label = "slow"
	case speed <= 90:
		label = "normal"
	default:
		label = "fast"
	}
	fmt.Println(label)
}
hints: Each of the first two parts is one `:=` line followed by one `if` with no `else`.
In the switch, check `speed < 40` first, then `speed <= 90`, and use `default` for fast.

recap:
- Go has no `cond ? a : b`, and `if` is a statement, so it cannot produce a value.
- Two outcomes: declare with `var x T`, then assign with `=` in if/else.
- One usual outcome: start at the default and override it with one `if`.
- Larger or smaller of two values: `bigger := a`, then `if b > a { bigger = b }`.
- Three or more outcomes: a `switch` with no value, `<` ranges ordered low to high, `default` last.
- Inside a branch use `=`, not `:=`, or you create a new variable that hides the outer one.
